📈 Our latest Senate forecast
Updated October 30, 2026
ELSEWHERE IN FLIPR:
Paid subscribers get full access to our Election Night livestream with The Argument, GD Politics, and Slow Boring.
This is the landing page the FLIPR1 2026 Senate forecast.2 This page is designed to be viewed on the web rather than in our email client or in the Substack app.
The Senate polls
The Silver Bulletin polling averages are the first step in FLIPR, so we reproduce them on every page.
We draw most of the election polls used in our model from The New York Times poll database3, but collect generic ballot and congressional approval polls ourselves.
The Senate forecast
Below, you’ll find our forecast for each 2026 Senate race, along with how our numbers have changed over time and which states are likeliest to decide control of the chamber.
manifold-02RzZt8EII.title: Silver Bulletin 2026 midterm Senate model

manifold-02RzZt8EII.text:
Ten days before the midterm elections, the battle for Congress is coming into focus, with Democrats favored to take the House but facing a more competitive fight for the Senate.
Democrats have a 95 percent chance of winning the House and a 76.4 percent chance of Senate control, according to the Silver Bulletin’s forecast, while VoteHub, Decision Desk HQ, and RealClearPolling averaging show a closer fight in the upper chamber.
Control of Congress matters now because November 3 will determine which party can advance legislation, lead committees, and scrutinize President Donald Trump during his final two years in office.
Read More on Politics
Voters in eight states – Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Maine, Michigan, South Carolina, and Texas – are positioned to have an outsized influence, with each Senate contest separated by fewer than four points in Nate Silver’s polling average.
Why It Matters
Midterms have historically created problems for the president’s party, as voters can use the election to check the White House without removing its occupant.
This year’s map suggests that backlash may extend beyond the House and threaten Republicans’ fragile 53–47 Senate majority.
What To Know
The following details were checked by Newsweek at 7 a.m.
ET on Friday, October 23.
Silver Bulletin updated its model on October 22 and projected an average Senate division of 52 Democrats to 48 Republicans.
VoteHub gives Democrats a 60 percent chance of controlling the Senate and projects a 52-48 chamber.
Decision Desk HQ puts the Democratic probability at 57 percent, with 51 seats, after running 1 million simulations.
Polling averages, such as that on RealClearPolling, measure current voter preference; forecasts add factors such as incumbency, political fundamentals, markets and uncertainty.
Alaska
Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman and the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress, is running in an unusual ranked-choice contest that also features a second Republican candidate named Dan Sullivan, something Trump said he was “very concerned” about in a Truth Social post this week.
Peltola leads incumbent Republican senator Sullivan by 3.5 points in Silver Bulletin, 48.1 percent to 44.6 percent.
RealClearPolling shows a narrower Peltola advantage of 1.2 points, based on surveys conducted from September 28 through October 16.
Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 61 percent probability and calls the race Lean Democratic.
Iowa
Democrat Josh Turek holds a 1.2-point Silver Bulletin edge over Republican U.S.
Representative Ashley Hinson, 46.8 percent to 45.6 percent.
Turek is a two-time Paralympic wheelchair-basketball gold medalist, while Hinson worked as a television news reporter before entering politics.
Other indicators underline the uncertainty: VoteHub has Turek ahead by only 0.3 points, whereas Decision Desk HQ projects Hinson to win by one point despite placing the contest in its toss-up category.
Kansas
Democrat Adam Hamilton leads Republican Senator Roger Marshall by 1.1 points in Silver Bulletin, with neither candidate reaching 47 percent.
Hamilton, the founder of a Methodist megachurch, has pitched himself as an independent-minded moderate in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator for nearly a century.
RealClearPolling instead gives Marshall a 0.3-point advantage, illustrating how a small change in methodology or included surveys can reverse the leader.
Decision Desk HQ rates Kansas Lean Republican and gives the GOP a 65 percent chance.
Ohio
Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown has a 3.7-point Silver Bulletin lead over Republican Senator Jon Husted, 48.1 percent to 44.4 percent.
The special election gives Brown a route back to the Senate two years after his defeat, while appointed incumbent Husted is seeking voter approval to complete the term originally won by JD Vance.
VoteHub finds a slightly wider 4.3-point margin, but Decision Desk HQ remains more cautious, giving Brown a 57 percent probability.
Maine
Democrat Troy Jackson stands at 49.6 percent against Republican Senator Susan Collins’ 46.8 percent in Silver Bulletin, putting Jackson 2.8 points ahead.
Jackson, a fifth-generation logger and former state Senate president, who entered the race as a replacement nominee after Graham Platner dropped out over allegations of sexual misconduct that he denies, is challenging Collins as the Republican seeks a sixth term.
The RealClearPolling average cuts that gap to 1.4 points, while Decision Desk HQ assigns Democrats a 56 percent chance.
Collins’ continued competitiveness leaves Maine among the model’s four true toss-ups.
Michigan
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers by three points in Silver Bulletin, 48.4 percent to 45.4 percent.
El-Sayed, a former Detroit health director with medical and public-health doctorates, faces former FBI agent and House Intelligence Committee chair Rogers.
VoteHub produces an almost identical 2.9-point gap.
RealClearPolling has El-Sayed ahead by 2, while Decision Desk HQ is more confident in the Democrat, giving the party a 68 percent probability.
South Carolina
Late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham’s sister Darline leads Democrat Annie Andrews by 1.7 points in Silver Bulletin, 47 percent to 45.3 percent.
Public polling is thinner here than elsewhere on the list, adding uncertainty to the average.
Decision Desk HQ nevertheless gives Graham, the appointed successor of the late Senator, a 70 percent chance and categorizes the race as Lean Republican.
Texas
Democrat James Talarico is 2.4 points ahead of Republican Ken Paxton in Silver Bulletin, 48.7 percent to 46.2 percent.
The contest pairs Talarico, a former public-school teacher, Presbyterian seminarian and state representative, with Paxton, the state attorney general who defeated incumbent Senator John Cornyn in the Republican runoff and was impeached by the state House in 2023 over allegations that he misused his office to help donor Nate Paul, before the state Senate acquitted him.
VoteHub places the margin at 2.5 points and RealClearPolling at 1.5.
Decision Desk HQ gives Talarico a 57 percent probability, making Texas a toss-up rather than a secure Democratic gain.
What Happens Next
No single average represents a prediction of the final result.
With 10 days remaining, small polling errors, turnout differences or late movement could still change both the individual winners and the party controlling the Senate.
Election Day is November 3.

midterm elections in November and called the unprecedented decision “regrettable”.

federal elections since the OSCE began observing in the country for which the OSCE has not received an invitation,” the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe’s Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights said in a press release.

Founded in 1975 to ease tensions between the East and the West during the Cold War, the Vienna-based OSCE counts 57 members from Europe, central Asia and North America.
It observes elections and has dispatched monitoring missions to conflict zones.

President Donald Trump’s administration, critical of how the OSCE handles its mission, has urged the OSCE to downsize its budget.

Federal judge allows some challenges to Trump's mail-in voting executive order
WASHINGTON (TNND) — A federal judge has allowed challenges to President Trump's mail-in voting executive order that apply to this year's elections.
Voter education nonprofits and Democratic-led states separately sued the Trump administration in April to block the executive order that the president signed in March, which also requires states to verify that only U.S.
citizens are registered to vote, The Hill reported.
On Thursday, U.S.
District Judge Indira Talwani, an Obama appointee, ruled that the plaintiffs must wait before raising concerns about elections beyond 2026.
She denied the administration’s request to dismiss all the claims, allowing challenges regarding the November midterms to continue.
The judge also determined that the court should not delay review due to the “ever-narrowing window of time” before the election and some states’ primaries.
“In light of the EO’s specific deadlines over the next three months, and the reality that elections will be occurring throughout this period with the November 3, 2026 midterm occurring in just five months, postponing judicial review is impracticable and may inflict significant hardship on Plaintiffs,” Talwani wrote in a 17-page consolidated order.
She also noted that there were “many uncertainties” as to how federal agencies would eventually implement the executive order, finding that it would be premature to challenge anything after the midterms.
“We are pleased that the Trump Administration’s attempt to dismiss our lawsuit as premature was rejected with respect to the upcoming November midterm elections,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta's (D) spokesperson told The Hill.
“The case will now move forward to a decision on the remaining disputed issues, and we remain confident that the law is on our side,” the spokesperson added.
Bonta’s office led the lawsuit from the states.
“The Trump Administration will continue to fight for the agenda the President was elected on – which includes the safety and security of our nation’s elections,” White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson said on Thursday.
“This very campaign pledge from the President is why millions of Americans sent him back to the White House.
Election security is common sense, and Democrats owe it to the American people to support the President’s mission to secure our elections.”
Trump's executive order directs Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to work with the Social Security Administration to compile a list of verified U.S.
citizens who are eligible to vote and prevents the U.S.
Postal Service from sending mail-in ballots to those not included.
The order also directed the attorney general to investigate and prosecute anyone accused of sending mail-in ballots to ineligible voters.
More than 20 states, Washington, D.C., and voting rights groups sued over the executive order, arguing that it was unconstitutional and threatened to disenfranchise eligible voters.
They also claimed in their lawsuits that the states, rather than the president, have authority over how federal elections are run.
The states also argued that the executive order would force them to invest “enormous amounts of time and resources” to comply and “sow confusion and chaos” in the election process.
“We are grateful the court recognized the urgency and stakes of this case and allowed our lawsuit to proceed with respect to this year’s elections,” the American Civil Liberties Union and other nonprofits said in a joint statement on Thursday.
“The court will now move to consider our preliminary injunction and other pending motions.
And we will continue to fight to protect the millions of people who rely on mail-in voting and to ensure that every eligible voter is able to fairly cast their ballot.”

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S.
Senator Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, released the following statement after the Trump Administration refused to invite international election observers to monitor the 2026 U.S.
midterm elections.
This marks the first time in more than two decades that the United States government is not inviting the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe’s (OSCE’s) Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) and the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly (OSCE PA) to observe the midterm elections.
“The Trump Administration’s decision not to invite international observers to the United States is deeply antithetical to the spirit of freedom, democracy and transparency that defines our elections.
The OSCE has observed every midterm election in the United States since 2002, and the Trump Administration’s failure to continue this practice is yet another step that risks undermining public trust in America’s safe and secure election system.
“I was an official election monitor in the country of Georgia in 2012 and most recently in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2022, so I know firsthand the importance of showing up for Allies and partners to improve the public’s confidence in election integrity.
The OSCE does just that.
It is a community—comprised of many of the United States’ closest allies—that has committed to hold each other to the highest standards of democracy and human rights.
I urge the Trump Administration to respect the role of independent election observers and ensure that the United States holds itself to the same standards that we would expect of any other democracy.”

The GOP and Democratic Party are both beefing up their legal teams to deal with potential election interference claims.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly challenged the results of the 2020 election, most recently on Thursday, saying that the “election was rigged.” He has also continued to claim he wants to ensure elections are safe from noncitizens illegally voting.

Multiple state courts are also dealing with redistricting questions that will affect the congressional maps voters use in 2028.
Despite the legal battles, election experts claim the voting process remains secure.
David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan nonprofit Center for Election Innovation & Research, assured voters that if they “can put the noise aside, what they’ll find is their voting process looks a lot like their voting process in 2024.”
“That it’s just as safe, that it’s just as convenient, that their options are there: early voting, mail voting, in-person voting,” Becker added.
Here are the top issues that are still pending before the Nov.
3 election.
Trump’s mail-in voting executive order sparks legal battle
The Supreme Court handed Trump a victory on Monday when it paved a path for his executive order limiting mail-in voting to be implemented.
Trump signed the order in March.
Two days later, U.S.
District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston handed Trump another victory by lifting an order that blocked the U.S.
Postal Service from implementing the executive order in time for the midterm elections.
Democratic state officials filed a challenge against the ruling, meaning the high court could issue a ruling before the November elections.
Talwani ruled late Thursday evening that the Postal Service’s plan to limit mail-in voting was onerous and would disenfranchise voters.
She blocked the plan from going into effect for 14 days.
A preliminary injunction hearing is expected to take place on Sept.
3.
Becker, the elections expert, said “it is now long past impossible for states and the Postal Service to effectively implement these extreme changes in time for the 2026 election without chaos, confusion, and disenfranchisement, which Judge Talwani recognized.
The clock is ticking, and it’s simply too late to implement any changes to election practice at this point, regardless of their merit or constitutionality.”
North Carolina is set to begin sending out ballots Sept.
4 overseas and to military voters, ratcheting up the stakes of the legal battle even as Trump insists his executive order is necessary.
“North Carolina is great … it’s a great place,” Trump told reporters on Thursday about how states can implement the order in time for the elections.
“I won it all three times,” Trump continued.
“They do some mail-in ballots, but basically they ruled on the legitimacy and the way we want to make them legitimate.
And it was a great ruling for the Republicans.”
Democrats counter the GOP’s efforts
Nearly two dozen Democratic attorneys general filed a lawsuit against the U.S.
Postal Service’s rules on mail-in voting.
The suit, filed in the U.S.
District Court for the District of Massachusetts, is co-led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and the attorneys general of Nevada, Washington state, and Massachusetts.
The Democratic National Committee, along with its sister committees, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, and Democratic Governors Association, also filed a preliminary injunction against Trump’s executive order this week.
“We will not stand by while Trump and Republicans try to unnecessarily inject chaos and confusion into our elections, just weeks before voting begins,” said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY), House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), DNC Chairman Ken Martin, DCCC Chairwoman Suzan DelBene (D-WA), DSCC Chairwoman Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), and DGA Chairman Andy Beshear (D-KY) in a joint statement.
In March, the DNC sued the Trump administration to determine whether armed personnel such as Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers or Border Patrol agents would appear at polling locations and ballot drop boxes.
The DNC alleged that 11 Freedom of Information Act requests filed to the Department of Justice were not met with adequate responses.
Last week, the DNC again sued the Trump administration over potential plans to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election materials before the midterm elections.
A DNC official said the committee requested the records to defend the integrity of our elections from attempts to seize lawfully cast ballots and to fight for the First Amendment right of eligible voters to have their voices heard.
The DNC cited the seizure of archived ballots from Fulton County, Georgia, in its lawsuit against the DOJ.
Redistricting cases still battling it out in states
The Supreme Court’s Louisiana v.
Callais decision earlier this year enabled southern states to eliminate several majority-minority districts through new congressional maps.
But several states are still battling over maps even with the midterm elections fast approaching.
Gov.
Wes Moore (D-MD) and allies faced defeat this week when Anne Arundel County Circuit Judge Robert J.
Thompson struck down a November ballot question for a state constitutional redistricting amendment.
The amendment would have allowed voters to decide whether or not to allow the Democratic-led General Assembly to redraw the state’s map, which likely would have eliminated the state’s only Republican congressman, Rep.
Andy Harris (R-MD), ahead of the 2028 elections.
The Missouri Supreme Court is also set to resolve a case about whether voters can challenge a congressional map via statewide petition.
A lower state court judge recently ruled that referendums do not apply to congressional maps.
The Missouri Supreme Court must act quickly; state law bars any addition to ballots after Sept.
8.
This week, the 11th U.S.
Circuit Court of Appeals sent a lawsuit over Georgia’s 2021 political maps back to a lower court to reexamine in light of the Callais decision.
The 2021 maps were accused of diluting black Georgians’ voting power, but in 2023 U.S.
District Judge Steve C.
Jones ordered the maps to be redrawn after he ruled that they violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, which has since been scaled back after the Supreme Court’s ruling in Callais.
“The appropriate response to such a significant change of law is to vacate and remand, so the district court may reconsider, in the first instance, whether Georgia’s redistricting plans violate Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act under the updated Callais framework,” the three-judge panel wrote.
Questions remain over committee and candidate coordination
The GOP faced a setback this week when the 4th U.S.
Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that coordinated ad buys between political parties and joint fundraising committees are not entitled to cheaper candidate rates.

“This was an incorrect ruling that ignores decades of precedent.
We plan on appealing, and this is the first word not the last,” Joanna Rodriguez, the National Republican Senatorial Committee communications director, told the Washington Examiner in a statement.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) publishes its first estimate of UK Gross Domestic Product (GDP) for the third quarter of 2026 on Thursday, November 12, 2026 at 7:00am London time (2:00am ET).
The release covers economic output for July, August and September 2026 and is typically published alongside the monthly GDP estimate for September.
Full background and the release schedule are available on the UK GDP hub page.
This is one of the most closely watched UK data points because it tells investors, the Bank of England and the government whether the economy grew, stagnated or shrank in the summer months, feeding directly into interest rate decisions and political debate about living standards.
What is GDP and why does it matter?
Gross Domestic Product measures the total value of all goods and services produced in the UK over a given period.
The ONS builds it from three angles, output (what industries produce), expenditure (what is spent by households, businesses and government) and income (wages, profits and taxes), which should in theory all arrive at the same total.
The headline figure that moves markets is the quarter-on-quarter percentage change in real GDP, meaning growth after stripping out the effect of inflation.
A positive number signals expansion, a negative number for two consecutive quarters is commonly, though informally, described as a recession.
Markets watch GDP closely because it is the single broadest gauge of economic health.
The Bank of England uses it, alongside inflation and wage data, to judge whether the economy has spare capacity or is running too hot, which in turn shapes decisions on interest rates that affect mortgages, savings and business borrowing across the UK.
It is also watched in Brussels, Frankfurt and Tokyo as one signal of demand for exports from the eurozone and Asia into the UK market.
When is the Q3 2026 GDP report released?
The ONS publishes the first quarterly estimate of Q3 2026 GDP, together with the monthly GDP estimate for September 2026, on November 12, 2026 at 7:00am UK time (2:00am ET).
The data is released on the ONS release calendar and in the GDP first quarterly estimate bulletin on the ons.gov.uk website.
This date follows the ONS’s standard pattern of publishing the first quarterly estimate roughly six weeks after the end of the reference quarter.
What is the consensus forecast?
As this release is still some way ahead, a consensus forecast for Q3 2026 GDP has not yet been published by data providers such as Reuters or Bloomberg.
Forecasts typically firm up in the days immediately before release, once monthly GDP prints for July, August and September have been published individually.
The most recent confirmed reading is the first quarterly estimate for Q2 2026 (April to June), published by the ONS on August 13, 2026, which showed real GDP grew by 0.4% quarter-on-quarter, in line with the median forecast in a Reuters poll, following growth of 0.6% in Q1 2026.
Nominal GDP rose by 0.8% in Q2 2026 and stood 4.1% higher than the same quarter a year earlier, according to the ONS bulletin.

| In line with consensus | A muted reaction is likely, since the print largely confirms what was already priced into markets by economists surveyed ahead of the release | The economy is behaving broadly as expected, so there is unlikely to be a big shift in mortgage rates or the pound on the day |
| Below consensus | Sterling could weaken and traders may increase bets on earlier Bank of England rate cuts, based on typical market reactions to weak growth surprises | Growth undershooting expectations often points to weaker hiring and spending, which can ease pressure on prices but also signals a softer labour market |
Why does this release matter right now?
The Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee weighs GDP growth against inflation and wage data when deciding on interest rates, so a Q3 2026 outturn that surprises in either direction could shift market expectations for the Bank’s next move.
Growth slowed slightly in the first half of 2026, from 0.6% in Q1 to 0.4% in Q2, according to ONS estimates, and commentators will be watching whether that gentle cooling continued into the summer or whether momentum picked back up.
The report also lands against a backdrop of ongoing debate about UK productivity, household spending power and the fiscal position ahead of any autumn budget measures, all of which tend to be discussed in relation to whatever the latest GDP figure shows.
What It Means for Your Money
Mortgages and borrowing: Stronger than expected growth can reduce the chance of near-term Bank of England interest rate cuts, which may keep mortgage and loan rates higher for longer.
Weaker growth can increase the odds of cuts, which could eventually feed through to cheaper borrowing.
Savings: Savings account and cash ISA rates tend to track the Bank of England’s base rate, so a weak GDP print that raises the chance of a rate cut could mean lower returns on cash savings over time, while a strong print could support current rates for longer.
Jobs and wages: GDP growth and employment tend to move together over time.
A run of weak GDP figures can be an early sign of slower hiring or wage growth, particularly in sectors sensitive to consumer spending such as retail and hospitality.
Prices: GDP does not directly set prices, but very weak growth combined with falling demand can help cool inflation, while strong growth in an economy already near capacity can add to price pressures.
Investments, pensions and currencies: UK shares, gilts and the pound can all move on the day of release.
A weaker pound following soft GDP data can make imports and overseas holidays more expensive for UK households, while making UK exports more competitive for buyers in Europe, Asia and the US.
Pension savers with UK-focused funds may see short-term movements in their portfolio values around the release.

UK economy grows 0.1% in August, defying forecasts of a decline
main article
The UK economy unexpectedly grew in August, with gross domestic product (GDP) edging up 0.1% from July as a jump in production offset flat services output and a decline in construction, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on 15 October.
According to Reuters, a poll of economists had forecast a 0.1% drop.
The increase in GDP follows unrevised growth of 0.4% in July, as well as growth of 0.4% in June, which was revised up from 0.3%.
The growth in August was driven by a 0.8% increase in production, with services showing no growth and construction falling by 0.2% over the prior month.
Compared with the same month a year ago, GDP is estimated to be 2.1% higher in August 2026.
This was the strongest figure since August 2022, when it grew by 2.6% annually.
In the three months to August 2026, real GDP grew by 0.7% compared with the three months to May.
“This is the eighth consecutive three-month-on-three-month growth and follows growths of 0.5% in both the three months to July 2026 and in the three months to June 2026,” the ONS said in a press release, adding that both July and June were revised up from 0.4% growth.
The largest contribution to the quarter-on-quarter growth came from the services sector, which grew by 0.9% in the three months to August 2026.
Notably, services increased by 0.5% month-on-month in June and July.
However, the construction sector fell 1.0% and production dipped 0.2% in August 2026.
Meanwhile, GDP is estimated to have grown by 1.8% in the three months to August 2026 compared with the same period a year ago.
Services grew by 2.2%, production was up by 0.8%, while construction fell by 1.6%.
The sectors with the largest contributions to year-over-year growth include professional, scientific and technical activities, and information and communication.

Updated 2 November 2026.
Brent crude is trading near $110 a barrel on Monday, down about 3 percent from Friday’s $113.43 January settlement (Trading Economics, 2 November); Reuters had Brent down 3.2 percent at $109.75 by 04:07 GMT.
OPEC+ kept December output targets unchanged on Sunday, as expected, so the drop is about Iran: Tehran says a Qatari-brokered plan could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days.
Verdict: the hold changed nothing; the risk premium is now trading on whether Washington answers the plan.
Reference levels: $104 below, $120 above.
Key facts
- Price: Brent near $110.06, down $3.37 on the day (Trading Economics).
Reuters: $111.84 at 00:11 GMT, down 1.40 percent, with WTI at $102.56 (via CNBC); $109.75 by 04:07 GMT, down 3.2 percent (via Finimize).
OilPriceAPI showed $110.05 at 06:31 GMT.
- Friday: Brent January settled at $113.43 and the expired December contract at $117.64.
Brent gained 13.6 percent in October (Reuters via our OPEC+ decision report).
- OPEC+: Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman kept December production targets unchanged at their online meeting on 1 November, a third straight monthly pause.
No further policy changes are expected until next year (Reuters via CNBC).
- What comes next for OPEC+: a review of members’ production capacity, now due by mid-November, and a meeting of all 21 members on 29 November that is expected to address the 2027 baselines (Reuters).
- Iran’s plan: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera that Qatar persuaded Tehran to shorten a seven-day plan to two days: US measures on day one, Hormuz reopened on day two.
Washington has not publicly responded (investingLive).
- Saudi exports: rose in October from September despite Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure, according to two of three ship-tracking companies (Reuters via CNBC).
OPEC+ held, and the market moved on
Our Sunday Brent page was written before the decision and argued that a hold was already in the price.
The first session confirmed it.
Brent opened lower and the slide deepened through the Asian morning, from about 1.4 percent at 00:11 GMT to more than 3 percent by 04:07 GMT.
Nothing in that move traces back to OPEC+.
The reason is the same one that has held since September: most Gulf producers still pump below their targets because of the war, so a target that is held, raised or cut barely changes the barrels on the water.
The real OPEC+ dates are the capacity review in mid-November and the 29 November meeting, where the 2027 baselines decide how the remaining cuts, about 2 million barrels per day for most members, are unwound.
The Hormuz plan, and its conditions
The oil move is about Iran.
Iranian and Qatari officials held a third straight day of talks on ending the US-Israeli war on Iran, with Pakistan also mediating (Reuters via CNBC, investingLive).
Araghchi’s two-day timetable is the most concrete proposal so far, but the conditions attached go to the core of the dispute: lifting recently imposed US sanctions, reinstating June oil waivers, a smaller US military presence, recognition of new shipping routes designated by Iran and Oman, an end to the conflict on all fronts including Israel’s attacks on Lebanon, and the release of frozen funds, including those held in Qatar (investingLive).
Washington’s response has been slow.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was not aware of a timeframe for a reply, and President Trump said he was in no great hurry to reach a deal.
Meanwhile, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed two more tankers struck mines in Hormuz on Sunday, a claim that has not been independently verified (investingLive).
What analysts say
Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade, called Monday’s fall a technical pullback after last week’s strong gains, helped by lingering hopes of diplomatic progress.
He also warned that rhetoric around Iran could be stepped up after Tuesday’s midterm elections and push Brent toward $120 (Reuters via CNBC).
ING said the next test is whether the geopolitical risk premium keeps fading without a major new strike or a breakthrough (via Finimize).
Even after today’s drop, Brent is up about 9.7 percent over the past month (Trading Economics).

|

| Between the bear case and Friday’s $113.43 settlement.
|
| Bull | $120 | Talks stall, the post-midterm rhetoric hardens or a confirmed strike hits shipping in the strait.

|
The bear case sits below Monday’s price.
These are reference levels measured from the verified spot, not forecasts.
What to watch
- A US reply to the Qatari-brokered plan.
Any public response is the fastest route to either end of the table.
- Tuesday 3 November: the US midterms, flagged by analysts as the point where Iran rhetoric could change.
- Tanker incidents in Hormuz: separate confirmed reports (UKMTO) from claims by the Revolutionary Guards.
- Mid-November: the OPEC+ capacity review, ahead of the 29 November meeting on 2027 baselines.
- Gold: cheaper oil is easing Fed hike bets, which is lifting gold today; see our Monday gold page.
Tuesday update: Brent settled at $104.77 on Monday, below this page’s bear case; our Tuesday Brent page covers the Qeshm strike report and the new levels.
Quick take: Brent is near $110 on Monday, down about 3 percent, after OPEC+ held December output as expected and Iran said a Qatari-brokered plan could reopen Hormuz in two days.
Washington has not answered and Iran’s conditions are steep.
Expect $106-$114 while talks continue; $104 needs real progress on the plan, $120 needs talks to stall after the midterms.
FAQ
What is the Brent crude oil price today?
Brent is trading near $110 a barrel on Monday 2 November, down about 3 percent from Friday’s $113.43 January settlement (Trading Economics, Reuters).
Why is oil falling today?
Iran and Qatar held a third day of talks on ending the war, and Iran’s foreign minister said a Qatari-brokered plan could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days.
Analysts also called the drop a technical pullback after last week’s gains (Reuters via CNBC, investingLive).
What did OPEC+ decide on 1 November?
Seven OPEC+ members kept December production targets unchanged, their third straight monthly pause.
No further policy changes are expected until next year (Reuters via CNBC).
When does OPEC+ meet next?
All 21 OPEC+ members meet on 29 November, when the group is expected to address 2027 production baselines after a capacity review due by mid-November (Reuters).
Why did Brent drop from $117.64 to $113.43?
It did not fall by that much.
$117.64 was the expired December contract’s final settlement; $113.43 is the January contract, now the front month.
The gap reflects the contract roll.

Tim Waterer of KCM Trade warned that rhetoric around Iran could push Brent toward $120 after the US midterm elections on 3 November (Reuters via CNBC).

Eastern Time today, the price of Bitcoin (1 BTC) is $77,750.64.

What is Bitcoin?
Bitcoin is the original cryptocurrency and remains the most popular crypto coin on the market.
Its market capitalization is around $1.33 trillion—considerably higher than the runner up, Ethereum, with a market cap of around $233 billion.
In short, it’s a decentralized digital currency.
What that means is that it’s run on a peer-to-peer network instead of being controlled by the government, a bank, etc.
It allows you to send value directly to someone else without a middleman.
Many people like the idea of investing in cryptocurrency as a potential hedge against the inflation of the U.S.
dollar—or simply as another way to diversify a portfolio.
Its growth has been enormous in the past decade, often trouncing the returns of major stock market indices, which is a big part of why investors find it so attractive.
But similar to other cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin is vulnerable to extreme volatility and sudden price fluctuations.
Bitcoin price history
Bitcoin has had a wild ride since its inception in 2009.
In its infancy, software developer and early Bitcoin believer Laszlo Hanyecz famously paid 10,000 Bitcoins for pizza.
Today, those coins would be worth over $668 million.
Over roughly the last decade, the cryptocurrency has had an astonishing rise—over 15,000%, in fact.
But its upside also comes with real risk, as cryptocurrencies tend to be wildly unpredictable.
Bitcoin has had some sharp dips, occasionally dropping tens of thousands of dollars in just a few months.
But it has also made similarly dramatic climbs.
In 2025, Bitcoin ended the calendar year dropping around 30% from its all-time high in October.
What affects Bitcoin’s price?
A variety of factors affect the price of Bitcoin, including:
- Investor speculation: As is the case with many investments, Bitcoin’s value is heavily influenced by trader sentiment and hype.
Its short-term demand is typically dictated more by investor hunches and speculative trading than anything else.
- Adoption by major companies: As companies adapt to crypto technology and Bitcoin starts to become a more accepted payment method, there is potential for considerable growth.
As an example, Bitcoin’s value increased after companies like Tesla and Ferrari announced they would begin accepting it as payment.
- Economy: Bitcoin isn’t as sensitive to inflation or Fed decisions as many other investments (stocks, for example).
But it does tend to increase in value when the U.S.
economy is doing well.
When people have money in their pocket, they tend to be more willing to explore alternative investments like crypto.
- Regulatory developments: Again, cryptocurrency is still relatively new.
Regulations are playing catch-up, and the decisions that are made can spook investors.
How to buy and invest in Bitcoin
You can invest in Bitcoin in several ways.
Here are some popular options.
Buy Bitcoin on a cryptocurrency exchange
Buying Bitcoin directly is one of the most popular ways to invest in cryptocurrency.
Just open an account with a cryptocurrency exchange and sync the account with your bank account to use your funds for Bitcoin.
Invest in Bitcoin ETFs
If you want to invest in Bitcoin without actually owning any yourself, you can instead look into a crypto exchange-traded fund (ETF).
A Bitcoin ETF is an investment fund that holds Bitcoin on your behalf, while its shares trade on stock exchanges like a regular stock.
You won’t have to set up a crypto account, and you won’t risk losing your crypto to lost passwords, wallet errors, or similar mishaps.
Buy crypto stocks
Another option for those wary of investing directly in Bitcoin is to invest in cryptocurrency-focused stocks.
Potential options include tech firms, publicly traded crypto exchanges, even payment processors.
They may use Bitcoin in their operations, so you’ll indirectly benefit from Bitcoin’s performance.
Open a Bitcoin IRA
For retirement-focused investors, a Bitcoin IRA can be a strong option.
Similar to a standard IRA, it’s a tax-advantaged account that allows you to use your retirement to purchase Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies.
Bitcoin IRAs have the same tax benefits and contribution limits as traditional or Roth IRAs, but you can invest in alternative assets.
Bitcoin vs.
other cryptocurrencies
Although Bitcoin is the most well-known cryptocurrency, it’s not the only investment option you have.
When deciding where to invest your money, consider these alternatives:
- Ethereum: After Bitcoin, Ethereum is the second-largest cryptocurrency.
And unlike Bitcoin, Ethereum wasn’t created to serve primarily as currency.
Instead, it was designed as a decentralized computing platform.
It’s a popular tool for developers.
- Tether: Tether is a stablecoin, meaning its value is tied to another asset.
In Tether’s case, its value is linked to the United States dollar.
As a result, Tether tends to be less volatile than Bitcoin, but that also means it lacks Bitcoin’s growth.
- XRP: XRP is a cryptocurrency specifically designed to move funds from one country to another quickly and with low fees.

Is it a good time to invest in Bitcoin?
Bitcoin is still relatively new when compared to blue chip stocks like Walmart, P&G, Coca-Cola, etc.
It’s hard to gauge how it’ll truly perform in the decades to come.
But it’s exhibited unbelievable performance in recent years.
And as the number of companies willing to accept it as payment increases, its price is likely to also increase.
As it becomes more established, it may experience fewer fluctuations in price, too.
As with any investment, you shouldn’t push all your chips into the middle of the table.
Put only money you won’t need in the near term into Bitcoin, and make sure the rest of your portfolio is diversified enough that other investments can help smooth out any sharp price swings.
All to say, Bitcoin is probably best thought of as a long-term investment—it’s not for those who spook easily.
If you plan on holding onto your investment for the long haul, investing money into Bitcoin, as just a part of a balanced portfolio, could be a good choice.

Some models price it at more than $700,000 by 2030, with conservative estimates closer to $300,000.

Can you buy a fraction of a Bitcoin?
Yes, you can buy a fraction of a Bitcoin.
Most cryptocurrency exchanges offer fractional investing, meaning you can buy portions of crypto coins.
Thanks to fractional investing, you can invest in Bitcoin with as little as a few dollars.
How do I start investing in Bitcoin as a beginner?
If you want to invest directly in Bitcoin by owning the currency, you’ll typically open an account with a cryptocurrency exchange.
Once the account is created, you can transfer money to your crypto account from your bank and place an order for Bitcoin and other tokens or coins.
You can also indirectly invest in Bitcoin via an ETF or a business that uses Bitcoin.
What can you buy with Bitcoin?
You can use your Bitcoin holdings in several ways, from selling for cash to trading it for other coins.
In some cases, you can also pay for purchases, such as with Tesla and Microsoft.

polymarket-6563871.text:
Bitcoin price enters November defending $76,000, the average cost basis of short-term holders.
The level was held after the Binance hack pushed BTC to a six-week low of $76,275.
The shock from Binance triggered $1.58 billion in liquidations, and BTC closed October with a 7% loss.
On-Chain Data Puts Bitcoin at a Make-or-Break Level
Glassnode data shows heavy exchange inflows during the late-October slide.
Net deposits reached about 11,500 BTC and 8,000 BTC on separate days, signaling sell-side pressure.
Net outflows of roughly 40,000 BTC followed within days, among the largest of 2026.
However, these flows do not suggest accumulation.
The stolen 18,270 BTC left a Binance hot wallet during the hack, which registers as an exchange outflow.
Users then pulled about $2 billion within three hours after withdrawals reopened on November 1.
Meanwhile, the attacker's coins remain untouched across 19 addresses.
Any move toward exchanges could add fresh supply pressure.
The Short-Term Holder Market Value to Realized Value (STH MVRV) ratio offers a clearer signal.
It compares the market price with the average cost basis of recent buyers.
The metric sits near 1.02, meaning short-term holders are about 2% in profit.
That places their cost basis close to $76,000, almost exactly at last week's low.
Historically, drops below 1.0 in 2026 preceded capitulation.
Breakdowns in late January and late May led to the February and June lows.
In contrast, the August reclaim sparked a rally toward $87,000.
The ratio has also printed lower highs since late September, falling from 1.20 to 1.03.
Holding $76,000 keeps recent buyers profitable, while losing it could push them to sell at a loss.
Bitcoin Price Prediction Points to Two November Scenarios
On the weekly chart, BTC is testing the bull market support band.
The band combines the 21-week exponential moving average (EMA) at $76,874 and the 20-week simple moving average (SMA) at $73,779.
However, the Gaussian channel has stayed red since March, signaling a broader downtrend.
BTC was recently rejected at the channel's declining midline, now near $81,850.
The weekly Relative Strength Index (RSI) reads 52, a neutral level that leans slightly lower.
The daily chart adds a bearish warning.
The Supertrend indicator flipped red after the hack, for the first time since May.
That May signal preceded a 25% drop to $57,800.
A similar decline from the latest flip near $80,000 would target roughly $60,000.
For now, BTC is holding the 0.5 Fibonacci retracement at $77,876.
Daily RSI has slipped to 38, extending a downtrend in momentum.
